chunks.title: Prediction Confidence Levels
chunks.content:
LunaBloom shows three confidence levels for its predictions:
- HIGH confidence: Shown when you have 3 or more completed cycles AND your cycle length variation (MAD) is 2 days or less. This means cycles are very regular and predictions are likely accurate.
- MEDIUM confidence: Shown when you have 2 or more cycles AND cycle variation is 5 days or less. Predictions are reasonable but may vary by a few days.
- LOW confidence: Shown when you have fewer than 2 cycles, or when cycle variation is high. This is normal for new users or those with naturally irregular cycles. Predictions will improve as more data is logged. LOW confidence does not mean the app is broken; it simply means more data is needed.

chunks.title: LunaBloom Prediction Engine
chunks.content:
LunaBloom predicts your next period using a weighted average of your historical cycle lengths.
1. It only uses completed cycles (where start and end dates are recorded).
2. It calculates the median of your recorded cycle lengths to avoid unusually long or short cycles skewing the result.
3. It applies Linear Weighted Moving Average (LWMA) with recency weighting, so recent cycles have more influence.
4. It uses Median Absolute Deviation (MAD) to detect and softly downweight outlier cycles instead of excluding them entirely.
5. Users can manually mark a cycle as 'exclude from predictions' if it was affected by unusual circumstances.
The next period start date is calculated as: most recent cycle start date + predicted cycle length.

chunks.title: Hormones Across the Menstrual Cycle
chunks.content: The menstrual cycle is driven by four main hormones: Estrogen, Progesterone, Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH), and Luteinizing Hormone (LH). Estrogen rises during the first half (follicular phase) to build the uterine lining. LH and FSH peak at ovulation to release an egg. After ovulation, progesterone rises during the luteal phase to prepare the uterus for potential pregnancy. If pregnancy doesn't occur, estrogen and progesterone levels drop, triggering menstruation.

chunks.title: PMS — Premenstrual Syndrome
chunks.content: Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) encompasses physical and emotional symptoms occurring in the days or weeks before a period. Common symptoms include bloating, breast tenderness, mood swings, fatigue, and irritability. These are linked to the natural rise and fall of hormones, particularly progesterone, during the luteal phase. Symptoms usually resolve shortly after the period starts.

chunks.title: PMDD — Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder
chunks.content: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) is a severe, sometimes disabling extension of PMS. While PMS involves physical and emotional symptoms, PMDD causes extreme mood shifts, severe depression, irritability, or anxiety that can disrupt daily life and relationships. Like PMS, it occurs during the luteal phase and resolves after menstruation begins.

chunks.title: Signs of Fertility
chunks.source: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG)
chunks.content: The 'fertile window' includes the days leading up to and including ovulation. Key physical signs include: 1. Cervical Mucus Changes: Mucus becomes clear, stretchy, and slippery (like raw egg whites) near ovulation to help sperm survive. 2. Basal Body Temperature (BBT): Body temperature slightly dips just before ovulation and rises sharply after ovulation due to progesterone. Tracking these signs helps identify when ovulation occurs.

chunks.title: Ovulation
chunks.content: Ovulation is the release of a mature egg from the ovary, typically occurring midway through the menstrual cycle (around day 14 of a 28-day cycle), triggered by a surge in Luteinizing Hormone (LH). Some individuals experience 'mittelschmerz'—a brief, mild pain on one side of the lower abdomen during ovulation. The egg survives for 12-24 hours.

chunks.title: Irregular Cycles
chunks.content: A cycle is considered clinically irregular if its length varies significantly from month to month (e.g., varying by more than 20 days), or falls outside the typical 21-35 day range. Common non-medical causes of temporary irregularity include high stress, extreme exercise, significant weight changes, travel, or starting/stopping hormonal birth control. Persistent irregularity can be related to conditions like PCOS or thyroid imbalances.

chunks.title: Menstrual Cramps (Dysmenorrhea)
chunks.source: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG)
chunks.content: Menstrual cramps (dysmenorrhea) are throbbing or cramping pains in the lower abdomen. They are caused by prostaglandins—chemicals made in the lining of the uterus that cause the uterine muscles to contract and shed the lining. Higher levels of prostaglandins are associated with more severe menstrual cramps. Primary dysmenorrhea is common menstrual pain, while secondary dysmenorrhea is caused by a condition like endometriosis or fibroids.

chunks.title: Perimenopause
chunks.content: Perimenopause means 'around menopause' and refers to the time during which a woman's body makes the natural transition to menopause. It can start in a woman's 40s or even late 30s. Symptoms include irregular periods (as ovulation becomes unpredictable), hot flashes, sleep problems, and mood changes. It lasts until menopause (defined as 12 consecutive months without a period).

chunks.title: Cervical Changes
chunks.content: The cervix changes position and texture throughout the cycle. Around ovulation, it typically becomes higher, softer, and more open (often summarized by the acronym SHOW: Soft, High, Open, Wet). After ovulation and during menstruation, it becomes lower, firmer, and closed. Cervical mucus also changes from dry/sticky to creamy, and finally to clear/stretchy during the fertile window.

chunks.title: The Luteal Phase
chunks.content: The luteal phase occurs after ovulation and before a period begins, typically lasting 11-17 days. The empty follicle that released the egg becomes a structure called the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone. Progesterone thickens the uterine lining. If a fertilized egg doesn't implant, the corpus luteum breaks down, progesterone levels drop, and the uterine lining sheds (menstruation).

chunks.title: The Follicular Phase
chunks.content: The follicular phase starts on the first day of menstruation and ends with ovulation. The pituitary gland releases Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH), prompting the ovaries to produce 5 to 20 follicles. Usually, only one follicle matures into an egg. As the follicle grows, it produces estrogen, which thickens the uterine lining in preparation for a potential pregnancy.

chunks.title: The Menstrual Phase
chunks.content: The menstrual phase is the first part of the cycle, commonly called a period. It occurs when an egg from the previous cycle is not fertilized. Estrogen and progesterone levels drop, and prostaglandins cause the uterus to contract and shed its thickened lining (the endometrium) through the vagina. A typical period lasts 3 to 7 days.

chunks.title: The Ovulation Phase
chunks.content: The ovulation phase is the shortest phase, lasting only 12 to 24 hours. Rising estrogen levels during the follicular phase trigger a spike in Luteinizing Hormone (LH). This LH surge causes the dominant follicle to rupture and release a mature egg. This is the only time during the cycle when fertilization can occur.

chunks.title: Mood and Hormones
chunks.content: Hormone fluctuations significantly impact mood. Rising estrogen in the follicular phase is often associated with higher energy and improved mood. After ovulation, the rise in progesterone can have a calming or sometimes sedative effect. The rapid drop in both estrogen and progesterone right before menstruation can trigger mood swings, irritability, or sadness (PMS).

chunks.title: Nutrition and the Cycle
chunks.content: Dietary needs can fluctuate with the menstrual cycle. During menstruation, iron-rich foods (like leafy greens and lean meats) help replenish iron lost through bleeding. In the luteal phase (before a period), magnesium-rich foods (like dark chocolate, nuts, and seeds) may help reduce cramping and improve mood. Staying hydrated is important throughout the cycle to minimize bloating.

chunks.title: Exercise Across the Cycle
chunks.content: Energy levels for exercise often track with hormones. During the follicular phase and ovulation, higher estrogen can increase energy, making it a good time for higher-intensity workouts (HIIT, heavy lifting). During the luteal phase and menstruation, energy may dip, making lower-intensity activities like yoga, walking, or light cardio more comfortable.

chunks.title: Sleep and Hormones
chunks.content: Hormone changes affect sleep architecture. The drop in estrogen and progesterone before menstruation can lead to poorer sleep quality, trouble falling asleep, or waking up frequently. Progesterone has a slight sleep-inducing effect, but its sudden drop can increase wakefulness. Maintaining good sleep hygiene and managing stress (which lowers cortisol) can help improve sleep quality during the luteal phase.
